question: What is the NCF for the Foundational Stage 2022 and what does it recommend for teaching 3–8-year-olds?
questionHi: बुनियादी स्तर के लिए NCF 2022 क्या है और 3–8 वर्ष के बच्चों के शिक्षण के लिए यह क्या सुझाता है?
keyPoints: Released October 2022 by MoE/NCERT (chaired by K. Kasturirangan committee); first of four NCFs under NEP 2020
Covers ages 3–8: Balvatika 1–3 and Classes 1–2
Five domains: physical, socio-emotional & ethical, cognitive, language & literacy, aesthetic & cultural; plus positive learning habits
Play as the central pedagogy — free, guided, structured play; conversations, stories, toys, songs, art
Panchaadi five-step process; Panchakosha view of development
Mother tongue (R1) as medium; assessment through observation and portfolios (no written tests)
Jaadui Pitara — play-based learning-teaching material
sampleAnswer: The NCF for the Foundational Stage was released in October 2022 as the first of the four curriculum frameworks under NEP 2020, covering ages 3 to 8 — Balvatika and Classes 1 and 2. It sets curricular goals across five domains: physical, socio-emotional and ethical, cognitive, language and literacy, and aesthetic and cultural development, plus positive learning habits. Its central recommendation is play as pedagogy — free, guided and structured play through conversation, stories, toys, songs, art and outdoor activity — and the Panchaadi sequence of Aditi, Bodh, Abhyas, Prayog and Prasar. It stresses the home language as medium, and assessment through observation, anecdotal records and portfolios rather than tests. NCERT's Jaadui Pitara is the play-based material kit that operationalises it.
followUps: What is Jaadui Pitara?
How is NCF-SE 2023 different from NCF-FS 2022?

question: What is experiential learning? Give an example from your primary classroom.
questionHi: अनुभवात्मक अधिगम क्या है? अपनी प्राथमिक कक्षा से एक उदाहरण दें।
keyPoints: Learning through direct experience followed by reflection (Kolb: experience → reflection → conceptualisation → application)
Dewey's learning by doing; NEP 2020 mandates experiential learning at all stages
Example must include reflection/discussion, not just an activity
Art-integrated, sport-integrated, toy-based, story-telling are recognised forms
sampleAnswer: Experiential learning means children learn by doing something and then reflecting on it — Kolb describes the cycle as concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation. NEP 2020 makes it a core pedagogy. For example, to teach measurement to Class 3, my students measured the classroom with hand-spans and got different answers. In the discussion afterwards they realised why we need a standard unit. Then they measured again with a metre scale and applied the idea to measure the corridor. The activity alone would be fun; the reflection is what produced the concept of standard units.
followUps: How is art-integrated learning different?
How would you assess learning in an experiential lesson?

question: What is competency-based education and how is it different from the traditional approach?
questionHi: सक्षमता-आधारित शिक्षा क्या है और यह पारंपरिक दृष्टिकोण से कैसे भिन्न है?
checking: Link to learning outcomes and assessment
keyPoints: Focus on what a child can DO with knowledge (competencies/learning outcomes), not chapter coverage
NCERT Learning Outcomes (2017) grade-wise; NCF-SE 2023 curricular goals → competencies
Mastery, flexible pace, application-oriented assessment
Traditional: content coverage, rote, marks; CBE: skills, understanding, transfer
Teacher plans backward from competency
sampleAnswer: Competency-based education focuses on what a child can actually do with what she learns — for example, 'reads a short text with comprehension' or 'solves daily-life problems using addition' — rather than on finishing chapters. NCERT's learning outcomes for each class and the curricular goals in NCF-SE 2023 define these competencies. In the traditional approach we cover content and test recall; in CBE we plan backward from the competency, allow children to reach mastery at a flexible pace, and assess through application tasks. So instead of asking 'Define a noun', I would ask children to find naming words in a poster they made.
followUps: Give a competency-based assessment task for Class 5 maths.
What is PARAKH?

question: How would you assess Class 2 children without giving them written tests?
questionHi: बिना लिखित परीक्षा कक्षा 2 के बच्चों का मूल्यांकन आप कैसे करेंगी?
checking: Knowledge of formative and authentic assessment
keyPoints: Observation with checklists/anecdotal records
Oral tasks, read-aloud fluency, show-and-tell
Portfolios of drawings and writing; worksheets as evidence
Peer and self-assessment (smileys, thumbs)
Holistic Progress Card (NEP 2020/NCF-FS) — 360° including parents and peers
Use results to adjust teaching (assessment for learning)
commonMistakes: Not connecting assessment back to teaching
sampleAnswer: For seven-year-olds assessment should be continuous and mostly invisible to the child. I would observe during activities using simple checklists and anecdotal records, listen to each child read aloud to note fluency, use show-and-tell and oral questions, and keep a portfolio of each child's drawings, writing and worksheets over the year. Children would also do simple self-assessment with smileys and peer feedback. I would record all this in the Holistic Progress Card format recommended under NEP 2020, which includes inputs from peers and parents. Most importantly I would use what I learn to regroup children and re-teach — assessment for learning, not just of learning.
followUps: What is an anecdotal record? Give an example.
How would you report progress to parents who expect marks?

question: What is your view on punishment in the classroom?
questionHi: कक्षा में दंड के बारे में आपका क्या विचार है?
keyPoints: Corporal punishment and mental harassment are banned — RTE Act Sec. 17; JJ Act 2015 Sec. 75
Discipline ≠ punishment; goal is self-discipline
Positive discipline: clear expectations, logical consequences, restorative conversation
Reinforcement more effective than punishment (Skinner)
Consistency and fairness
sampleAnswer: Corporal punishment and mental harassment are prohibited under Section 17 of the RTE Act and the Juvenile Justice Act, and beyond the law I believe punishment damages the trust that learning needs. My goal is self-discipline. I use positive discipline — clear expectations set with children, logical consequences such as repairing what was spoiled, restorative conversations about how behaviour affected others, and consistent reinforcement of good choices. For example, if a child scribbles on a desk, cleaning it and talking about shared property teaches more than standing outside the class.
followUps: What is the difference between a consequence and a punishment?
What if parents ask you to be strict with their child?

question: What is the RTE Act 2009 and what are its main provisions?
questionHi: RTE अधिनियम 2009 क्या है और इसके मुख्य प्रावधान क्या हैं?
keyPoints: Gives effect to Article 21-A; in force 1 April 2010; free and compulsory education for 6–14 years
25% seats for disadvantaged/EWS in private unaided schools (Sec. 12(1)(c))
No detention till Class 8 (amended 2019 to allow states to detain in Class 5/8 after re-exam); no board exam till Class 8
No corporal punishment/mental harassment (Sec. 17); no capitation fee/screening (Sec. 13)
Norms: PTR 30:1 (Classes 1–5), infrastructure, teacher qualifications (NCTE), 45-hour work week, CCE
SMC with 75% parents; School Development Plan
commonMistakes: Saying no-detention still applies everywhere unchanged
sampleAnswer: The RTE Act 2009 operationalises Article 21-A and came into force on 1 April 2010. It guarantees free and compulsory elementary education to every child aged 6 to 14 in a neighbourhood school. Key provisions: 25 per cent reservation for disadvantaged children in private unaided schools under Section 12(1)(c); no screening or capitation fee for admission; no corporal punishment or mental harassment under Section 17; originally no detention till Class 8, though the 2019 amendment allows states to hold back children in Classes 5 and 8 after a re-examination; continuous and comprehensive evaluation; norms like a pupil-teacher ratio of 30:1 at the primary level and NCTE-prescribed teacher qualifications; and School Management Committees with at least three-fourths parents, which prepare the School Development Plan.
followUps: What is your view on the no-detention policy?
How does RTE affect KVs?

question: What is PM SHRI and how does it relate to Kendriya Vidyalayas?
questionHi: पीएम श्री क्या है और यह केंद्रीय विद्यालयों से कैसे संबंधित है?
keyPoints: PM Schools for Rising India — approved 7 Sept 2022; 14,500+ schools to be developed as exemplar NEP 2020 schools
Includes KVs and JNVs along with state schools
Green school, ICT/smart classrooms, experiential and competency-based learning, vocational exposure, holistic assessment
Mentorship for nearby schools
Many KVs have been designated PM SHRI schools
sampleAnswer: PM SHRI — PM Schools for Rising India — was approved in September 2022 to develop more than 14,500 existing schools as exemplar schools that showcase NEP 2020: green infrastructure, smart classrooms and ICT, experiential and competency-based pedagogy, vocational exposure and holistic assessment, and mentoring of nearby schools. Kendriya Vidyalayas and Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas are part of it, and a large number of KVs have been designated PM SHRI schools. As a PRT in such a school I would be expected to actually practise play-based and competency-based teaching and use the Holistic Progress Card, not just know about them.
followUps: Name two 'green school' practices you could start in a primary wing.
What is Samagra Shiksha?

question: You are transferred to a KV in a remote area with poor infrastructure. How will you react?
questionHi: आपका स्थानांतरण कम सुविधाओं वाले दूरस्थ क्षेत्र के KV में हो जाता है। आप कैसे प्रतिक्रिया देंगी?
keyPoints: Transfers are part of KVS service; accept professionally
Low-cost/no-cost TLM from local materials; community resources
Focus on what matters — teacher quality is the biggest factor
Use local culture and environment as curriculum resource
Stay connected professionally (ZIET, DIKSHA)
commonMistakes: Saying you would seek immediate re-transfer
sampleAnswer: Transfers are part of serving in KVS and I would accept it as a professional. Infrastructure matters, but research consistently shows the teacher matters more. I would make low-cost TLM from local materials — seeds, stones, bottle caps for maths, and the local environment for EVS — involve the community and parents, and use the local culture as a resource for language and art. I would stay professionally connected through the regional office, ZIET training and DIKSHA. Frankly, such postings often teach a teacher the most.
followUps: What if there is no electricity for your digital plans?
How would you support your own family during such a posting?

question: A child in your class comes from another state and does not understand Hindi or English well. How will you help?
questionHi: आपकी कक्षा में दूसरे राज्य से आया एक बच्चा हिंदी या अंग्रेजी अच्छी तरह नहीं समझता। आप कैसे मदद करेंगी?
keyPoints: Common in KVs — children of transferred employees
Welcome and emotional safety first; buddy who may share the language
Visuals, gestures, TPR, bilingual labels; value his language in class
Gradual language support; parents as resource
NEP 2020 multilingualism; do not penalise for language in other subjects
commonMistakes: Treating it as the child's deficiency
sampleAnswer: This is exactly the situation KVs exist for, so I would first make him feel welcome — learn a few words of his language, let him teach the class a greeting, and give him a buddy, ideally one who shares his language. I would use visuals, gestures and TPR, label the classroom bilingually, and let him show understanding through drawing or actions while his Hindi grows. I would talk with his parents about what he already knows academically, so that I assess his maths or EVS understanding fairly rather than his language. Following NEP 2020's multilingual spirit, his language would be treated as a resource for the whole class.
followUps: How would you assess his maths knowledge fairly?
How would you involve other children?

question: How would you use Vygotsky's ideas of scaffolding and ZPD while teaching reading?
questionHi: पढ़ना सिखाते समय आप वायगोत्स्की के स्कैफोल्डिंग और ZPD के विचारों का उपयोग कैसे करेंगी?
keyPoints: ZPD: what child can do with help; scaffolding: temporary support gradually withdrawn
Gradual release: modelled (I do) → shared (we do) → guided (you do with me) → independent (you do)
Read-aloud → shared reading with big book → guided small groups by level → independent reading
Peer tutoring with more capable peers; language as tool of thought — talk about text
Fade support as fluency grows
commonMistakes: Not showing the withdrawal of support
sampleAnswer: Vygotsky says learning happens in the zone between what a child can do alone and what she can do with help, and scaffolding is the temporary support we give in that zone. In reading I follow a gradual release model. First I model — reading aloud and thinking aloud about the picture and the words. Then shared reading with a big book, where the class reads with me and I point to each word. Then guided reading in small groups formed by reading level, where children read and I prompt only when needed. Finally independent reading from the class library. More capable peers act as reading buddies. The key is that the support is removed step by step as each child's fluency grows — otherwise it is not scaffolding but dependence.
followUps: How would you form guided reading groups?
What prompts would you use when a child is stuck on a word?
source: Vygotsky; Pearson & Gallagher gradual release model

question: What is the difference between a teaching method and a teaching strategy? Which methods suit primary classes?
questionHi: शिक्षण विधि और शिक्षण युक्ति में क्या अंतर है? प्राथमिक कक्षाओं के लिए कौन सी विधियाँ उपयुक्त हैं?
keyPoints: Method: overall approach (play-way, activity, project, storytelling, demonstration, inductive-deductive)
Strategy/technique: specific tactic within a method (questioning, think-pair-share, role play, brainstorming)
Primary: play-way (Froebel/Montessori), activity-based, storytelling, learning by doing (Dewey/Kilpatrick), toy-based (NEP)
Choice depends on objective, age and content
commonMistakes: No distinction between method and strategy
sampleAnswer: A method is the broad approach to organising learning — such as play-way, activity method, project method or storytelling — while a strategy or technique is a specific tactic used inside it, like think-pair-share, role play, brainstorming or questioning. For primary classes the most suitable are play-way, which comes from Froebel and Montessori; activity-based and learning-by-doing from Dewey and Kilpatrick; storytelling; demonstration; and toy-based and art-integrated learning recommended by NEP 2020. I choose based on the learning outcome, the age of the children and the content — for example storytelling for values in Class 1 and a small project for the theme 'food' in Class 4.
followUps: Explain think-pair-share with an example.
When would you use demonstration?

question: Do you have any questions for us? / Is there anything else you would like to add?
questionHi: क्या आप हमसे कुछ पूछना चाहती हैं? / क्या आप कुछ और जोड़ना चाहेंगी?
keyPoints: Thank the board
One brief, thoughtful question (e.g., induction/mentoring for new PRTs, FLN initiatives in the region) — or politely decline
Optionally one sentence re-affirming commitment
Do not ask about salary/leave/transfer preferences
sampleAnswer: Thank you for this opportunity and for your time. I would like to ask one thing: what induction or mentoring support does KVS provide to new PRTs in their first year? And I would just add that whatever the outcome, this conversation has strengthened my commitment to foundational-stage teaching.

question: What are your strengths and weaknesses as a teacher?
questionHi: एक शिक्षक के रूप में आपकी ताकत और कमजोरियाँ क्या हैं?
keyPoints: Two strengths with brief evidence
One genuine weakness (not a disguised strength) + what you are doing about it
Avoid weaknesses that are core to the job (e.g., 'I lose patience with children')
sampleAnswer: My strengths are planning and creativity — I prepare every lesson around an activity and low-cost TLM, and children in my classes are rarely passive. A genuine weakness is that I sometimes take on too much myself instead of delegating to children or colleagues, which affects my time. I am working on it by giving children classroom responsibilities and by using a weekly planner, and my mentor has noticed the improvement.
followUps: How do you handle feedback from your principal?

question: Two children in your class are always fighting with each other. How will you resolve it?
questionHi: आपकी कक्षा में दो बच्चे हमेशा आपस में लड़ते रहते हैं। आप इसे कैसे सुलझाएँगी?
keyPoints: Separate calmly; listen to both individually then together
Help each express feelings ('I felt…') and understand the other — restorative approach
Agree on a solution and a signal for future
Cooperative tasks where they depend on each other
Monitor; involve parents if persistent
sampleAnswer: I would first calm the situation and later hear each child separately, then bring them together in a short restorative conversation where each says what happened and how they felt, and listens to the other. We would agree together on how to handle the next disagreement — perhaps a signal to come to me. Then I would deliberately give them cooperative tasks where they need each other, such as a joint chart, because shared success changes relationships. I would monitor for a few weeks and involve the parents if it continues.
followUps: What if one child is clearly the aggressor each time?

question: What do you know about the Holistic Progress Card (HPC)?
questionHi: समग्र प्रगति कार्ड (HPC) के बारे में आप क्या जानती हैं?
keyPoints: Recommended by NEP 2020 (para 4.35) to replace marks-based report cards
Developed by PARAKH (NCERT) for Foundational, Preparatory and Middle stages
360°, multidimensional: self, peer, teacher and parent inputs; competencies across domains
Descriptive, strengths-based; tracks progress not just achievement
Being adopted by CBSE schools including KVs
sampleAnswer: The Holistic Progress Card comes from NEP 2020, which asked for report cards to become holistic, 360-degree, multidimensional records of progress. PARAKH at NCERT has developed HPC formats for the foundational, preparatory and middle stages. It includes the teacher's observations, the child's self-assessment, peer feedback and parents' inputs, and describes competencies across domains — cognitive, socio-emotional, physical, creative — rather than giving marks. It tracks growth over time and strengths, and CBSE schools including KVs are moving to it. For me it means keeping systematic observations and portfolios throughout the year.
followUps: How would you get meaningful input from parents for the HPC?

question: What co-scholastic activities would you like to lead in a KV and why are they important?
questionHi: KV में आप कौन सी सह-शैक्षिक गतिविधियों का नेतृत्व करना चाहेंगी और वे क्यों महत्वपूर्ण हैं?
keyPoints: KVS culture: Bal Sabha, morning assembly, Scouts & Guides (Cubs/Bulbuls at primary), sports meets, art, music, reading campaigns, Ek Bharat Shreshtha Bharat activities
NEP 2020: no hard separation between curricular and co-curricular
Own skill — music, art, storytelling, sports
Benefits: confidence, teamwork, values, talent identification
commonMistakes: Treating co-scholastic as 'extra' or less important
sampleAnswer: KVs have a rich co-scholastic life — morning assembly, Bal Sabha, Cubs and Bulbuls under Scouts and Guides, sports meets, art and music, and Ek Bharat Shreshtha Bharat activities. I would like to lead the primary reading club and storytelling, and help with Bulbuls, because I enjoy music and stories. NEP 2020 removes the hard line between curricular and co-curricular, and for good reason: these activities build confidence, teamwork, values and language, and often reveal talents that never show in a test.
followUps: How would you use the morning assembly for learning?

question: What is the difference between NCF 2005 and NCF-SE 2023?
questionHi: NCF 2005 और NCF-SE 2023 में क्या अंतर है?
keyPoints: NCF 2005: under NPE 1986; constructivism, learning without burden, connecting to life, flexible exams; 10+2 structure
NCF-SE 2023: under NEP 2020; 5+3+3+4 stages; competency-based curricular goals; multilingualism; rootedness in India; 360° assessment; two board exams a year; flexibility of subjects at secondary
Continuity: child-centred, constructivist spirit
sampleAnswer: NCF 2005 was framed under the National Policy on Education 1986. It brought constructivism into Indian classrooms — connecting knowledge to life outside school, moving away from rote learning, reducing curriculum load and making exams flexible — within the 10+2 structure. NCF for School Education 2023 is framed under NEP 2020. It adopts the 5+3+3+4 stages, defines competency-based curricular goals for each stage, emphasises multilingualism and rootedness in Indian knowledge, and reforms assessment towards holistic, 360-degree evaluation. The child-centred, constructivist spirit continues; what changes is the structure, the explicit competencies and the assessment system.
followUps: What does NCF-SE 2023 say about the Preparatory Stage that concerns you as a PRT?

question: How will you ensure every child participates, including the shy and quiet ones?
questionHi: आप कैसे सुनिश्चित करेंगी कि हर बच्चा, विशेषकर शर्मीले और शांत बच्चे, भाग लें?
keyPoints: Low-risk participation: think-pair-share, whiteboards/slates for all, thumbs up/down
Wait time; no-hands-up random selection with support
Small groups and roles; pair shy child with a supportive peer
Non-verbal options: drawing, pointing, acting
Build relationship and safety; praise attempts
Track participation
commonMistakes: 'I will call on them directly' only
sampleAnswer: I would design participation so that it is low-risk. Everyone answers on slates or shows thumbs up or down; children first discuss in pairs before anyone speaks to the class; and I give wait time. Shy children get a supportive partner and a role in the group, and can respond by drawing, pointing or acting rather than speaking at first. I make a point of praising attempts, not just correct answers, and I quietly keep a tally of who has participated so no child goes unnoticed for a week.
followUps: What is wait time and why does it matter?

question: How is a KVS PRT's role different from a private school primary teacher's role?
questionHi: KVS PRT की भूमिका निजी विद्यालय के प्राथमिक शिक्षक से कैसे भिन्न है?
keyPoints: Diverse, mobile student population from across India — national integration
All subjects at primary level; NCERT/CBSE; uniform academic calendar
Government responsibilities — records, schemes, RTE compliance, Scouts/Guides, exam duties
Structured CPD via ZIETs, NISHTHA; transferability
Same core: child's learning and well-being
sampleAnswer: The core is the same — the child's learning and well-being. What is distinct in KVS is first the diversity: children come from every state and often move mid-year, so the teacher is an agent of national integration and must handle transitions with care. Second, a PRT teaches all subjects following NCERT and a uniform national calendar, with structured professional development through ZIETs and NISHTHA. Third, there are institutional responsibilities — maintaining records, implementing schemes and RTE norms, Scouts and Guides, and being ready for transfer. I am prepared for this breadth and see the diversity as the most rewarding part.
followUps: How would you settle a child who joins in the middle of the year?

question: What is PARAKH and why was it created?
questionHi: PARAKH क्या है और इसे क्यों बनाया गया?
keyPoints: Performance Assessment, Review and Analysis of Knowledge for Holistic Development — national assessment centre under NCERT, set up 2023 as recommended by NEP 2020 (para 4.41)
Sets norms and guidelines for student assessment across boards; equivalence of boards
Conducts large-scale surveys (National Achievement Survey / PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan)
Developed the Holistic Progress Card
Aims to shift assessment from rote to competency
sampleAnswer: PARAKH stands for Performance Assessment, Review and Analysis of Knowledge for Holistic Development. It is the national assessment centre set up under NCERT in 2023 as recommended by NEP 2020. Its job is to set norms and guidelines for student assessment across all school boards, bring equivalence among boards, conduct large-scale achievement surveys such as the PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan, and steer assessment away from rote memorisation towards competencies. It also developed the Holistic Progress Card. For a primary teacher, PARAKH's work defines how I will assess and report children's progress.
followUps: What was the National Achievement Survey and what did it show about foundational learning?
